# Session 0: Introduction to the Course {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Reproducibility

> **How many bioinformaticians does it take to change a light bulb?** One, but first they write a pipeline for it, and then it only works on their own laptop.
:::

## What this course is about

KB8029 brings two subjects together: **bioinformatics**, the computational analysis of biological sequences and structures, and **machine learning**, in particular the neural networks behind today's methods. They are not taught as two separate halves. The classical bioinformatics methods motivate the machine learning, and the machine learning is applied to the same biological problems.

![The course at a glance. Sessions 1-2 refresh the mathematics and programming the rest of the course uses. Sessions 3-6 cover classical bioinformatics: databases, alignment, database searches with profiles, and protein structure. In Sessions 7-9 the two subjects meet: a profile score turns out to be a simple neural network, and the networks are trained properly. Sessions 10-12 cover modern deep learning, up to AlphaFold. One problem, predicting protein structure from sequence, runs through the second half and ends in your capstone project.](figs/session00-roadmap.png){width="100%"}

By the end of the course you should be able to

- find, retrieve and compare biological sequences and structures using the main databases and tools;
- explain how the classical methods work: alignment, substitution matrices, profiles and database searches;
- build, train and evaluate neural networks in PyTorch, and judge whether a result is real;
- explain how modern deep-learning methods for proteins work, from convolutional networks and protein language models to AlphaFold;
- design, train and evaluate your own secondary-structure predictor (the [capstone project](capstone.qmd)).

The full plan is on the [Course Schedule](schedule.qmd) page.

## How a session works

Each of the twelve sessions has the same parts:

| Part | Where | What it is for |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **The page** | this book, e.g. [Session 1](session01.qmd) | the material of the session, with self-study questions and a short quiz at the end |
| **The course notebook** | this book, linked from each page, with an "Open in Colab" badge | the same material in code; read it, then run and change it |
| **The lecture** | on site | explanations, live coding, and short **discussion problems** you work on in groups (notebooks opened by QR code) |
| **Live quizzes** | [quiz.bioinfo.se](https://quiz.bioinfo.se), on your phone | quick questions during the lecture, to check what has landed |
| **The lab** | a separate lab notebook in this book, questions on [Canvas](https://canvas.su.se/) | most sessions; hands-on work with real data, submitted as a short online quiz |

Read the page before the lecture: the lectures assume you have seen the material once, and use the time for the parts that are hard to learn alone. **Lectures are not recorded.**

## People

The course has two teachers, one for machine learning and one for bioinformatics, and teaching assistants who run the lab sessions. This year's teachers and teaching assistants are listed on Canvas.

Ask questions in the Canvas discussion forum, where everyone can see the answers. The teaching assistants help during the scheduled lab hours; do not expect immediate help at other times.

## The rules, in brief

To pass, you need to pass all the **labs**, the **capstone project** (a secondary-structure predictor of your own: a Colab notebook, a short report, and an oral presentation of your code to a teaching assistant) and the **exam**. Your work must be your own, and AI tools may help you understand but must not write your labs or report. The grading, the grade scale, and the rules on plagiarism and AI tools are on the [Course Information & Logistics](course-info.qmd) page.

## At SciLifeLab

The lectures and labs are at SciLifeLab in Solna. You need a SciLifeLab access card to enter and leave the building; when and where to collect it is announced by email or on Canvas.

- Use your card **every time** you pass the speed gates, on the way in and on the way out.
- The gates let **one person through at a time**. To let a visitor in, use your card twice, with a few seconds in between, or the alarm goes off.
- Never force your way through a gate.

## Computers

You can do almost everything on your own laptop. Some labs use the course server, which you reach with an **SSH key**, and the heavier computations use **Google Colab**, which gives free access to a GPU. The [Setup](setup.qmd) page takes you through all of it: creating and sending your SSH key, connecting VS Code to the server, and running notebooks on Colab. Session 6's lab uses **PyMOL** to look at protein structures.

If you do not have a laptop that can do this, tell us now, not on the day of a lab.

## Before Session 1

1.  Accept the course invitation on [Canvas](https://canvas.su.se/), and check the schedule there.
2.  Work through the [Setup](setup.qmd) page: create an SSH key and send the public key, and make sure you can open a notebook in Colab.
3.  Open [quiz.bioinfo.se](https://quiz.bioinfo.se) on your phone and check that you can log in.
4.  Read the [Session 1](session01.qmd) page, the mathematics refresher, and try its practice problems.

## What's next

[Session 1](session01.qmd) refreshes the mathematics the course relies on: vectors and matrices, derivatives and gradients, and probability, likelihood and entropy. [Session 2](session02.qmd) does the same for programming in Python.
